title: Job 5:1–16
context: Job 5:1–16 continues the speech of Eliphaz. He tells Job that no holy one will answer his appeal, and he describes how resentment and jealousy destroy the foolish, whose children and harvest are lost. Trouble does not spring from the ground, he says, but humans are born to trouble as sparks fly upward. If he were Job, he would seek God and commit his cause to him, the God who does great and unsearchable things, sends rain, lifts up the lowly, frustrates the crafty, and saves the needy. Eliphaz’s line that God takes the wise in their own craftiness (5:13) is quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 3:19: "He has taken the wise in their craftiness." Both traditions note that Paul’s use shows the statement is true about God, while the book as a whole shows that Eliphaz applies true principles wrongly to Job’s case. These remain Eliphaz’s words, and the book’s later verdict (42:7) shapes how they are read.

verses.text: “Call now; is there any who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz tells Job to call out, but asks whether anyone will answer and to which of the holy ones he will turn. Arminians see Eliphaz suggesting that Job’s appeal for vindication is useless.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the holy ones as heavenly beings. Both traditions note that Job will later long for a mediator or witness (9:33; 16:19), and they read this verse as Eliphaz’s words.

verses.text: For resentment kills the foolish man, and jealousy kills the simple.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says resentment kills the foolish and jealousy kills the simple. Arminian readers see a true wisdom saying, but they sense that Eliphaz may be warning Job against his complaints.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the principle is true in general. Both traditions note that Eliphaz may be implying that Job’s lament is foolish resentment, and they read the verse as his perspective, not the book’s verdict.

verses.text: I have seen the foolish taking root, but suddenly I cursed his habitation.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says he saw the foolish taking root, but suddenly he cursed his dwelling. Arminians see Eliphaz describing how the apparent prosperity of the wicked is short-lived.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see a common wisdom theme (compare Psalm 37:35–36). Both traditions note that Eliphaz’s observation is true in some cases but becomes harmful when applied to Job’s losses.

verses.text: His children are far from safety. They are crushed in the gate. Neither is there any to deliver them,
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the children of the foolish are far from safety and crushed in the gate with no one to deliver them. Arminian readers note the painful implication for Job, whose children had died (1:18–19).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the words as especially harsh in Job’s situation. Both traditions read the verse as Eliphaz’s general claim, which he applies without compassion, and which the book’s verdict does not endorse.

verses.text: whose harvest the hungry eat up, and take it even out of the thorns. The snare gapes for their substance.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the hungry eat the harvest of the foolish and the snare gapes for their wealth. Arminians see the picture of loss continuing, which Eliphaz presents as the fate of the foolish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the verse may echo Job’s own losses (1:13–17). Both traditions read it as part of Eliphaz’s argument, and they avoid treating it as the book’s explanation of Job’s suffering.

verses.text: For affliction doesn’t come out of the dust, neither does trouble spring out of the ground;
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says affliction does not come from the dust, and trouble does not spring from the ground. Arminian readers see him stating that trouble has causes and is not random.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the claim as true in that nothing happens apart from God. Both traditions note that Eliphaz is implying a moral cause for Job’s trouble, which the book’s opening chapters show is not the case.

verses.text: but man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upward.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says humans are born to trouble as sparks fly upward. Arminians see a true observation about the human condition in a fallen world, which both traditions affirm.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the proverb as describing the reality of life after the fall. Both traditions read the verse as one of Eliphaz’s statements that is true in general, while noting that it does not explain Job’s particular suffering.

verses.text: “But as for me, I would seek God. I would commit my cause to God,
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says that if he were Job, he would seek God and commit his cause to him. Arminian readers see good advice in itself, since turning to God in trouble is always right.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the counsel as sound in principle. Both traditions note that Job does seek God throughout the book, and that Eliphaz’s advice assumes Job needs to repent of sin, which the book does not confirm.

verses.text: who does great things that can’t be fathomed, marvelous things without number;
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz describes God as doing great things that cannot be fathomed, marvelous things without number. Arminians see a true description of God’s greatness, which Job himself affirms (9:10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as praise of God’s unsearchable works. Both traditions read it as true in itself, and they note that the LORD’s speeches later display his wonders far more fully (chapters 38–41).

verses.text: who gives rain on the earth, and sends waters on the fields;
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God gives rain on the earth and sends water on the fields. Arminian readers see God’s care for creation, which shows his goodness to all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s providence in sustaining the world. Both traditions read the verse as a true statement about God, shared ground that is part of Eliphaz’s larger argument.

verses.text: so that he sets up on high those who are low, those who mourn are exalted to safety.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God sets the lowly on high and lifts mourners to safety. Arminians see God’s compassion for the humble and grieving, a theme throughout Scripture (compare 1 Samuel 2:7–8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign power to reverse circumstances. Both traditions read the verse as true, and they note that it anticipates Job’s eventual restoration, though not for the reasons Eliphaz assumes.

verses.text: He frustrates the plans of the crafty, so that their hands can’t perform their enterprise.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God frustrates the plans of the crafty so their hands cannot carry them out. Arminian readers see a true statement about God’s opposition to the schemes of the wicked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over human plans. Both traditions read the verse as true in itself, while noting that Eliphaz is building a case against Job that the book does not support.

verses.text: He takes the wise in their own craftiness; the counsel of the cunning is carried headlong.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God takes the wise in their own craftiness, and the counsel of the cunning is carried headlong. Arminians note that Paul quotes this line in 1 Corinthians 3:19, which shows that the statement is true about God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see Paul’s use as confirming the truth of the saying. Both traditions note that a true statement can still be misapplied, as Eliphaz does in Job’s case, and they read the verse in light of 42:7.

verses.text: They meet with darkness in the day time, and grope at noonday as in the night.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the crafty meet darkness in the daytime and grope at noon as at night. Arminian readers see a vivid picture of the confusion God brings on those who rely on their own cleverness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the image as describing God’s judgment on human pride. Both traditions treat the verse as part of Eliphaz’s true but misapplied description of God’s ways.

verses.text: But he saves from the sword of their mouth, even the needy from the hand of the mighty.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says God saves the needy from the sword of their mouth and from the hand of the mighty. Arminians see God’s care for the poor and oppressed, a true and important theme in Scripture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God as the defender of the weak. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about God’s justice, while noting that it is spoken by Eliphaz within a larger argument.

verses.text: So the poor has hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: Eliphaz says the poor have hope and injustice shuts her mouth. Arminian readers see hope for the oppressed, grounded in God’s justice, which is a true and encouraging statement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as summarizing God’s care for the needy. Both traditions read it as true in itself, while recognizing that Eliphaz uses it to urge Job toward a repentance the book does not require.
